issues.description: The Bitmap24::set() method's parameter names disagree between the header and the implementation: the header declares the method parameters as (int i_x, int i_y, char i_r, char i_g, char i_b) while the implementation defines it as set(int i_y, int i_x, char i_r, char i_g, char i_b). Although the parameter types and order are the same (so the code compiles), the inconsistent parameter names (and the header's apparent x/y ordering) conflict with the usage in main (bitmap.set(i, j, ...)), which treats the first argument as the row (y) and the second as the column (x). This naming mismatch is a structural inconsistency that can confuse students about the intended coordinate order (x,y vs y,x) and lead to misunderstandings when they implement or use the API.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the parameter naming and documentation consistent across header and implementation. For example, change the declaration in Bitmap24.hpp to use the same parameter names as the implementation (e.g. set(int i_y, int i_x, ...)) or change the implementation to match the header (and update internal indexing accordingly). Additionally, add a short comment in the header clarifying the expected argument order (e.g. // i_y: row, i_x: column) so students are unambiguous about coordinate ordering.

issues.description: The Bitmap24::set parameter ordering/names differ between the template header and the implementation/solution: the template header declares set(int i_x, int i_y, ...) while the implementation (in Bitmap24.cpp) and the solution header use set(int i_y, int i_x, ...). This mismatch on the same conceptual parameters (row vs. column / y vs. x) can confuse students about the coordinate order when calling set and may lead to incorrect pixel placement.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the parameter order and names consistent across header and implementation. For example, change the template header declaration to match the implementation/solution: void set(int i_y, int i_x, char i_r, char i_g, char i_b); and document that the first parameter is the row (y) and the second is the column (x).
